script: "Micro‑dosing my child with raw chicken? I never imagined the fallout…". I was working from home, coffee in one hand, a mini‑fridge in the corner of my office. I'd been hitting Celsius a lot, feeling like a power‑hacker. The little door on the freezer popped off a week ago—thought it was nothing. Turns out, I'd been building a giant ice block in my fridge for days. Yesterday, I had had enough. I shut the fridge down, let it defrost, and fixed the door. After a few hours, I ended up with a chunk of ice, about 8 by 6 inches, half an inch thick. I tossed the wet towels in the washer, dumped the ice into the sink, and went back to work, feeling like I'd conquered a minor apocalypse. My husband came home, decided we'd have chicken for dinner, opened a couple of packs, and poured the excess water—like a little chicken juice—into the same sink. He started cooking while I kept working. The ice sat there, dripping and smelling faintly of chicken. Then our 7‑year‑old wandered in. You'd think she'd be smart enough to skip that sink, but she didn't. She started eating the ice right off the kitchen sink. I have no idea how much she ate or whether any chicken was on it, but the risk was there. My husband walked in from the bathroom and caught her in the act. He freaked out. The sink was scrubbed and disinfected, but the damage was done. We scrubbed her with antibacterial soap and a strong mouthwash, gave her a lecture about eating from the sink (or the trash can, just in case). Now we're on high alert, watching for any signs of food poisoning. She's been fine for 26 hours so far. I swear, if I'd stayed off the Celsius and just been lazy, none of this would have happened.
